turns.en: so to avoid melting one of the things we were doing was constantly rewriting the whole search and indexing and query serving system to be more efficient and use different data structures and you know more compact representations of things. And we got to a point in 2001 where we realized that that the way we were sort of scaling both the index size and the amount of capacity we had for serving the index was we would make more and more partitions of the index. We called them shards to have a bigger index. And then every one of those shards you would make more and more copies of it to provide capacity for serving more queries uh simultaneously. Um, and we eventually got to the point where we had, you know, instead of seven shards and 10 copies each, we had like 60 shards and 20 copies of each in every data center. And we eventually did the math and realized that we could put instead of having the the index on disk, we could put the entire index of the web in memory on the 1200 machines that would otherwise be 20 copies of the 60 partitions. And that was that was really fun. We we sort of sped up all of our search system by like 4x in uh three days which was pretty fun.
turns.zh: 为了避免融化，我们做的一件事就是不断重写整个搜索、索引和查询服务系统，使其更高效，使用不同的数据结构和更紧凑的表示。2001 年我们意识到，我们扩展索引大小和服务容量的方式是制作越来越多的索引分区。我们称之为分片，以获得更大的索引。然后每个分片你会制作越来越多的副本，以提供同时服务更多查询的能力。嗯，我们最终达到了这样的程度：不是 7 个分片每个 10 个副本，而是每个数据中心有 60 个分片每个 20 个副本。我们最终算了一下，意识到我们可以把整个网络索引放在内存中，而不是放在磁盘上，放在 1200 台机器上，这些机器原本是 60 个分区的 20 个副本。那真的很有趣。我们在三天内将整个搜索系统加速了约 4 倍，这很有趣。

turns.zh: 当时我们的数据中心里有 CPU，所以有很多 CPU，我们用了大约 16,000 个 CPU 核心来训练一个大型视觉模型，我们得到了这些惊人的改进，我们也为语音模型这样做。模型的质量提升惊人。我们在大约两个月内尝试构建深度声学语音模型，在词错误率方面取得了相当于过去 20 年语音研究的改进。嗯，所以那就像是，天哪，这将会非常好。但我们如何服务它？当时我做了一些计算，我说好吧，假设 1 亿人每天对着手机说话几分钟。那么我们如何服务？结果发现，仅仅为了在 Google 一个不起眼的小部分推出更好的语音识别模型，我们就需要将 Google 的计算机数量翻倍。那似乎有点过分。更不用说不可行了。所以我们决定专用硬件是出路。这就是 TPU 系列的起源，我们想构建专用加速器，基本上非常擅长低精度线性代数，仅此而已。然后这样你就可以更高效地服务系统，比如语音模型和视觉模型等等。结果发现，在 2015 年我们有了芯片时，它的每瓦性能比当时的 CPU 和 GPU 好 30 到 80 倍。

turns.zh: 是的。是的。我的意思是，作为机器学习开发者或研究者，你想要的就是能够表达你的高层次想法，然后让它神奇地在大规模系统上运行，而不必过多考虑为了获得良好性能可能需要在底层做的所有性能相关的事情。所以这意味着要有一个好的编译器、非常好的互连、能够表达抽象概念的框架，比如我是在和本地机器上的四块芯片打交道，还是在和大型分布式设置中的一万块芯片打交道。你希望不必过多考虑这些。针对这两种设置做不同的事情。

turns.en: So talk about the iterations of different TPUs and where do you see it all going?
turns.zh: 那么谈谈不同 TPU 的迭代，以及你认为这一切将走向何方？

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. So I mean then after TPUv1, which is really just a PCIe card that fit in a slot, and then we actually bought a whole bunch of those without knowing how we would use them. I cornered our CFO at the time and said we need to buy a lot of these because we're going to use them. We're not sure what for, but can we please buy a lot? So we did. And then TPUv2 was kind of the first system that we designed with training in mind, right? With not just a single chip but a whole sort of supercomputer-like system of many chips interconnected with a 2D torus. Over the generations we've introduced liquid cooling starting in TPUv3, so it's always exciting when you have pipes going to the surface of your chips in your system—leaks are not a good thing. And then TPUv4 as you scaled up the pod size—TPU 2 and 3 had fixed wiring between 256 chips and then 1,024 chips—and then as you start to get larger and larger systems, then you start to have failures in individual chips or boards or systems and you need to be more fault tolerant because you still want to be able to use the whole topology of a much larger pod even if something's broken. And so TPUv4 introduced this notion of an optical reconfigurable network between racks of machines. And so you can sort of assemble like Lego bricks from all over the data center floor, right? With funny little switches that have little micro-adjustable mirrors to make it seem as though these eight racks are right next to each other even though they're scattered across many aisles in the data center. And then that's been super useful. TPU v5 and 6 and 7 all introduce lower and lower precision computational formats, which has been super useful. You get much higher performance from that. Although it's always weird to compare flops when some flops are 16-bit and some are 8-bit and some are 4-bit. If you can make use of them in your machine learning algorithms, the lower precision ones are a really great way to get even more performance.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。我的意思是，在 TPUv1 之后，它真的只是一块插在插槽里的 PCIe 卡，然后我们实际上买了一堆这样的卡，却不知道我们会怎么用它们。我当时堵住了我们的 CFO，说我们需要买很多这样的卡，因为我们会用到它们。我们不确定用来做什么，但能不能请让我们多买一些？所以我们买了。然后 TPUv2 是我们第一个以训练为设计目标的系统，对吧？不仅仅是单个芯片，而是一个类似超级计算机的系统，由许多芯片通过二维环面互连。在几代产品中，我们从 TPUv3 开始引入了液冷，所以当你的系统中有管道通向芯片表面时总是很刺激——泄漏可不是好事。然后 TPUv4 随着 pod 规模的扩大——TPU 2 和 3 在 256 个芯片和 1,024 个芯片之间有固定布线——然后当你开始构建越来越大的系统时，你就会开始遇到单个芯片、板卡或系统的故障，你需要更具容错性，因为即使某些东西坏了，你仍然希望能够使用更大 pod 的整个拓扑。所以 TPUv4 引入了机架之间光学可重构网络的概念。这样你就可以像乐高积木一样从数据中心各处组装，对吧？用有趣的小开关，带有微调反射镜，让这八个机架看起来像是紧挨着的，尽管它们分散在数据中心的许多过道中。然后这非常有用。TPU v5、6 和 7 都引入了越来越低的精度计算格式，这非常有用。你可以从中获得更高的性能。尽管当一些 flops 是 16 位、一些是 8 位、一些是 4 位时，比较 flops 总是很奇怪。如果你能在机器学习算法中利用它们，低精度的那些是获得更高性能的绝佳方式。

turns.en: And then so the first TPU was 2015, 2017 was when the paper came out. It's just legendary now. And then 2018 Pathways—let's talk about Pathways a little bit and why that's so important.
turns.zh: 那么第一块 TPU 是 2015 年，2017 年论文发表。现在它已经是传奇了。然后 2018 年的 Pathways——让我们稍微谈谈 Pathways 以及为什么它如此重要。

turns.en: Yeah. So we started to build Pathways really to handle training of much more irregular and much sparser models and also as the underlying system infrastructure for it to enable us to have a single programming model, a single sort of process that would be driving a large distributed training system. So it's much nicer as a programmer if your single Python process just looks like it has 8,000 devices attached to it and you're like, great, I just want to do an all-reduce across all 8,000 devices and it will do that without you having to do anything special. And the underlying software in both the XLA compiler does some of that and then at the slightly higher level Pathways orchestrates data movement between lots of different chips. So you have chips within the same TPU pod and if you need to communicate there it'll use the ICI high-speed links that are in the TPU pod. But if you then need to have something that spans multiple pods or you need to talk from this chip on this pod to this chip on this pod, then Pathways will orchestrate that transfer using the data center network or even a wide area network if you're cobbling together a training job of pods in Oklahoma and Texas and Iowa or something. And then that kind of just gives you this nice abstraction of I just have a whole bunch of compute and I'm going to allow the system to figure out how best to use it.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们开始构建 Pathways 真的是为了处理更加不规则和更加稀疏的模型的训练，并且作为底层系统基础设施，使我们能够有一个单一的编程模型、一个单一的进程来驱动大型分布式训练系统。所以作为程序员，如果你的单个 Python 进程看起来就像连接了 8,000 个设备，那就好多了，你会说，太好了，我只想在所有 8,000 个设备上做一个全归约，它就会做到，而不需要你做任何特殊的事情。底层软件中，XLA 编译器做了一些工作，然后在稍高的层次上，Pathways 编排许多不同芯片之间的数据移动。所以你在同一个 TPU pod 内有芯片，如果你需要在那里通信，它会使用 TPU pod 中的 ICI 高速链路。但如果你需要跨多个 pod 或者需要从这个 pod 上的芯片与那个 pod 上的芯片通信，那么 Pathways 将使用数据中心网络甚至广域网来编排该传输，如果你把俄克拉荷马州、德克萨斯州和爱荷华州等地的 pod 拼凑成一个训练任务的话。然后这给你一个很好的抽象：我有一大堆算力，我将让系统找出最佳使用方式。

Now I think you're very deeply involved in designing the Gemini models, the current Gemini models and future Gemini models as well.

turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think the whole set of TPU generations has really benefited from the fact that we are big users of the ML compute ourselves and we have lots of people trying to push the boundaries of new research ideas that might stress the hardware in ways that existing workloads don't. And so by having everything under one sort of Alphabet roof, I guess, we actually can have a lot of interaction between the future TPU generation designers, the software designers of the compilers and the infrastructure, and then the machine learning researchers who can say hey, you know, this kind of thing seems to be working at small scale.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，我认为整个 TPU 系列确实受益于我们自己就是 ML 算力的大用户，我们有很多人试图推动新研究想法的边界，这些想法可能会以现有工作负载没有的方式对硬件造成压力。所以通过将所有东西都放在 Alphabet 这个屋檐下，我想，我们实际上可以在未来的 TPU 代际设计师、编译器和基础设施的软件设计师，以及机器学习研究者之间进行大量互动，研究者可以说嘿，你知道，这种东西似乎在小规模上有效。

turns.en: We think that's going to be really important for large-scale future training runs in a year or two, and we want to make sure our hardware does that. Because as a computer architect, if you're doing this in isolation, just trying to guess where the fast-moving AI field is going in the two-to-six-year time frame that your particular chip you're designing now has to be relevant in, it's super hard. And the more insight you can get, the better.
turns.zh: 我们认为，这对未来一两年的大规模训练运行非常重要，我们要确保我们的硬件能做到这一点。因为作为计算机架构师，如果你闭门造车，只是去猜快速发展的 AI 领域在未来两到六年会走向哪里，而你眼下设计的这款芯片必须在那时仍然有用，这超级难。你能获得的洞察越多越好。

turns.en: Yeah, we think this thing will work. And the more actual iteration — it's not just like we think we need to do this. It's often like the hardware people say, well, that's hard, but we could do this. Would that be useful? And you have this kind of back and forth of like, yes, that would actually enable us to do something very close to this, or maybe even better.
turns.zh: 对，我们认为这东西能行。而且迭代越多——不只是我们觉得需要这么做。经常是硬件那边的人说，这很难，但我们可以这么做，那会有用吗？然后就有这种来回的讨论：对，那实际上能让我们做到非常接近这个的事，甚至可能更好。

turns.en: Yeah. And that's super important for making effective chip design.
turns.zh: 对。这对做出有效的芯片设计超级重要。

turns.en: Yesterday I was on stage and gave the opening. I was talking about, as we start to ramp up and scale up Gemini models, right? I remember every single month we sit in the same meetings to talk about reliability. So I'm on the infra side, and Jeff represents GDM demand. We say, hey, you know what, the Gemini model becomes bigger and bigger, then we use tons of TPUs to train the models. Eventually we use 100,000 TPUs to train the models. That's the one metric we're looking at together, which is called goodput.
turns.zh: 昨天我在台上做了开场演讲。我讲到，随着我们开始逐步扩大 Gemini 模型的规模，对吧？我记得每个月我们都坐在同样的会议上讨论可靠性。我在基础设施这边，Jeff 代表 GDM 的需求方。我们说，嘿，你知道吗，Gemini 模型越来越大，然后我们用大量 TPU 来训练模型。最终我们用 10 万个 TPU 来训练模型。我们一起看的就是一个指标，叫有效算力利用率（goodput）。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: Goodput. Then initially our goodput is not good. I remember what we said together —
turns.zh: 有效算力利用率。一开始我们的有效利用率并不好。我记得我们一起说——

turns.en: badput dominates goodput. So initially like 60%. As we scale up more and more TPUs to pre-train that model, it becomes very complicated. We need bigger scale. We need more data. We need more parallelism. The goodput was like in the beginning 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, but it's just not good enough, right?
turns.zh: 无效利用率压过了有效利用率。所以一开始大概 60%。随着我们用越来越多的 TPU 来预训练那个模型，事情变得非常复杂。我们需要更大的规模，需要更多数据，需要更多并行。有效利用率一开始是 50%、60%、70%、80%，但就是不够好，对吧？

turns.en: But the long story short, now we use much more massive-scale training infrastructure to train much more complicated models, and it can be as high as 95%, even 98%.
turns.zh: 但长话短说，现在我们用规模大得多的训练基础设施来训练复杂得多的模型，有效利用率可以高达 95%，甚至 98%。

turns.en: Yeah. And I think that's actually a combination of a whole bunch of things, like better operational practices, better QA testing of the chips when they're deployed, software things that can deal better with failures and continue to make forward progress even if some part of the system is down. All these things together matter a lot and make a big difference.
turns.zh: 对。我认为这实际上是很多因素共同作用的结果，比如更好的运维实践、芯片部署时更好的质量检测，以及软件层面能更好地处理故障，即使系统某部分宕机也能继续向前推进。所有这些加在一起非常重要，带来了很大差别。

turns.en: Yeah, I think that's also another benefit. If we own the model, we own the data, we also own the entire hardware, networking and all the software stack, that actually gives —
turns.zh: 对，我觉得这也是另一个好处。如果我们拥有模型、拥有数据，也拥有整个硬件、网络和所有软件栈，那实际上就给了——

turns.en: and the operations team like —
turns.zh: 还有运维团队，就像——

turns.en: You can say, hey, it's super important, because if you think about an individual tray of TPUs, if you don't think that's part of a larger system, you're like, okay fine, we can repair that in a week when we sweep by here. But if it's part of a pod that is being used and there are many broken trays in it, then you want to go fix them like immediately, because the blast radius of the thing you need to repair is actually much bigger than it might seem.
turns.zh: 你可以说，嘿，这超级重要。因为如果你只看单独一个 TPU 托盘，不把它当成更大系统的一部分，你会觉得，行吧，我们一周后顺路过来修就行。但如果它是一个正在被使用的 pod 的一部分，里面有很多坏掉的托盘，那你就想立刻去修，因为需要修复的东西的影响范围其实比看起来大得多。

turns.en: So when you're talking about 100,000 chips, reliability really isn't a software patch problem anymore. Would you say it's more of a system design? Is it more related to physics?
turns.zh: 所以当你说到 10 万块芯片时，可靠性真的不再是一个软件补丁的问题了。你觉得它更多是系统设计问题吗？还是更多与物理有关？

turns.en: I mean, I think reliability is really a property of a whole system, and there are many different things you want to make robust. Like one thing you can do is make robust wholes out of unreliable parts. Right. This is actually from the very beginning of Google. We bought like cheap consumer PCs to serve our search traffic, and we made robust system software systems on top of that, right? That would enable us to handle individual machine failures and still give the functionality that whatever system was on it was supposed to be providing. Maybe it's a distributed file system, so you replicate data across multiple machines and you always have some that are available even if some of the replicas of a piece of data are down. And I think you can do the same thing in large-scale AI training systems. If you have a 20-pod default configuration, but one of them is down, you can make progress with 19 of the pods while you're repairing the 20th.
turns.zh: 我是说，我认为可靠性确实是整个系统的一种属性，有很多不同的东西需要你做得健壮。比如你可以做的一件事，是用不可靠的部件搭出可靠的系统。对。这其实从 Google 最早的时候就开始了。我们买便宜的消费级 PC 来服务搜索流量，然后在上面构建健壮的系统软件，对吧？这样我们就能处理单台机器的故障，同时仍然提供那个系统本该提供的功能。也许它是一个分布式文件系统，所以你把数据复制到多台机器上，即使某份数据的某些副本挂了，你总有一些是可用的。我认为在大规模 AI 训练系统里也可以做同样的事。如果你有一个 20 个 pod 的默认配置，其中一个挂了，你可以在修复第 20 个的同时用 19 个 pod 继续推进。

turns.en: And Bill, you kind of touched on this a little bit yesterday with your keynote about OCS and Virgo. Do you want to talk a little bit about that and how that plays into reliability?
turns.zh: Bill，你昨天在主题演讲里谈到 OCS 和 Virgo 时也稍微提到了这一点。你要不要聊一聊，以及它如何影响可靠性？

turns.en: Yeah, I think there's a long journey. I think the first thing is we look at every interrupt — every single 10,000 chips, every single part — how many interrupts per day we have, right? We have to minimize that, because if there are too many interrupts as we scale up the training cluster, there are way too many interrupts, that's not very good, right? So one thing we did is, okay, how can we improve the hardware reliability? Right.
turns.zh: 对，我认为这是一个漫长的过程。我想第一件事是，我们看每一次中断——每一万块芯片、每一个部件——每天有多少次中断，对吧？我们必须把它降到最低，因为随着训练集群规模扩大，如果中断太多，那就不太好了，对吧？所以我们做的一件事就是，好，我们怎么提高硬件可靠性？对。

turns.en: Then not only do we do that, but also — yesterday I was mentioning that even before pre-training starts, we actually look at all — we actually did some software. So software actually scans the entire fleet, right, every single component, what's your vital sign. If the vital sign is actually somewhat problematic, we actually either fix it or exclude it before we even start training. That's the first thing, right?
turns.zh: 然后我们不仅做这个，而且——昨天我提到，甚至在预训练开始之前，我们实际上会看所有——我们实际上做了一些软件。软件会扫描整个集群，对吧，每一个组件，你的生命体征如何。如果生命体征有点问题，我们实际上要么修好它，要么在训练开始之前就把它排除掉。这是第一件事，对吧？

turns.en: The second thing is, training gets started, but when training gets started, even if the hardware shows very, very strong vital signs, right, the training starts — I mean training lasts for weeks, it can still have problems, right? Then still can have problems. How can we identify which specific components and servers have problems, then fix that, then exclude it, replace it, and fix that? That's the second thing.
turns.zh: 第二件事是，训练开始了，但训练开始后，即使硬件显示出非常非常强的生命体征，对吧，训练开始了——我是说训练持续好几周，仍然可能出问题，对吧？仍然可能出问题。我们怎么找出哪些具体的组件和服务器有问题，然后修好它，再把它排除、替换、修好？这是第二件事。

turns.en: Now also, as Jeff mentioned, there's a lot of operational coordination, right? If the data center is maintaining the entire power — this data center role — then this role is actually doing the training. That's of course not very good. So we actually coordinate a lot with the data center and the setups and the site reliability engineers and all the ML researchers and engineers. That's a lot of coordination.
turns.zh: 另外，正如 Jeff 提到的，有很多运维上的协调，对吧？如果数据中心在维护整个电力——这个数据中心的角色——而这边这个角色实际上在做训练，那当然不太好。所以我们实际上要和数据中心、和搭建团队、和站点可靠性工程师以及所有机器学习研究员和工程师做大量协调。这是大量的协调工作。

ts.sec: Fault Tolerance and Silent Data Errors

turns.en: We have to be in sync. I think Jeff also led a lot on the general model design and on the software design side. I think sometimes things got failed.
turns.zh: 我们得保持同步。我觉得 Jeff 在整体模型设计和软件设计方面也主导了很多工作。我觉得有时候确实会出故障。

turns.en: You know what, actually the training actually is the data parallelism and model parallelism together. If that's within one data replica, the one replica maybe there's a case — you know what, the additional replica just keep going, right? You just average weights automatically, so you don't have to be bothered by this one replica going down, right? So it's a lot of very comprehensive improvements.
turns.zh: 其实训练本身就是数据并行和模型并行的结合。如果这都在一个数据副本里，那一个副本也许会有情况——你知道，额外的副本就继续跑，对吧？你只要自动对权重取平均，所以不必为某一个副本挂掉而操心，对吧？所以这是很多非常全面的改进。

turns.en: Anything to add there?
turns.zh: 有什么要补充的吗？

turns.en: No, I mean I think there's all kinds of things that can happen and it's very hard to predict every possible way something might fail. So also building robust things that can detect failures even though you're not necessarily sure what caused the failure, but you can detect it, right? Like so you know occasionally you have chips that when maybe when the temperature goes up they start to have unreliability problems — like they add two plus two and get five or something. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没有，我是说我觉得可能发生各种各样的情况，很难预测每一种可能的故障方式。所以也要构建健壮的东西，能够检测故障，即使你不一定清楚故障的成因，但你能检测到它，对吧？比如偶尔有些芯片，当温度升高时就开始出现不可靠的问题——比如二加二得五之类的。是的。

turns.en: And you want to be able to detect that because that's not great if you're —
turns.zh: 你得能检测到这种情况，因为那可不妙，如果你——

turns.en: That's the most nasty one. That's a silent data error. That's horrible, that's horrible.
turns.zh: 那是最讨厌的一种。那是静默数据错误。太可怕了，太可怕了。

turns.en: Yeah. And that can happen in the chip itself. It can happen in a flaky network link. It can happen lots of places. So yeah, you know, even we're using a lot of the same principles we used in the very early days of Google where, you know, because we bought these cheap consumer PCs, they not only didn't have ECC, they didn't have parity in their memory. And so if you use a lot of computers to do something and none of them have parity —
turns.zh: 是的。这可能发生在芯片本身，可能发生在不稳定的网络链路上，可能发生在很多地方。所以，你知道，我们甚至在沿用 Google 早期用的很多原则——因为当时我们买的是便宜的消费级 PC，它们不仅没有 ECC，内存里连奇偶校验都没有。所以如果你用很多台电脑做一件事，而它们都没有奇偶校验——

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Then you are going to get random bit flips in things. And so a lot of the computations we did, you know, you wanted to be robust to bit flips, and one of the ways you could do that was you could be like, fine, I'm processing a billion web pages, if I drop one of them it's probably not the end of the world, so you could just ignore that by checksumming in software above the hardware layer to make things robust even if you know a particular machine or maybe the network link or whatever was not reliable.
turns.zh: 那就会随机出现比特翻转。所以我们做的很多计算，你希望对比特翻转有鲁棒性，而做到这一点的方法之一是，你可以说，行，我在处理十亿个网页，丢掉一个大概也不是世界末日，所以你可以在硬件层之上的软件里做校验和，把这件事忽略掉，让系统保持健壮，即使某台机器或者网络链路之类不可靠。

turns.en: Now, Google is a big believer in open source. So I'm going to shift gears a little bit to talk about open source. And I know we have a lot of academics in the audience. We have a lot of our partners as well. So let's talk a little bit about Google's AI infrastructure strategy as it relates to making sure that it's not a gated resource. So all these things that we talk about, we want to make sure that we're sharing it with the world. So let's talk about like JAX and StableHLO and that evolution of open source as a whole and how is that so relevant today to ensure that this doesn't become a gated resource.
turns.zh: Google 非常信奉开源。所以我要稍微换个话题，谈谈开源。我知道观众里有很多学者，也有很多我们的合作伙伴。那我们就聊聊 Google 的 AI 基础设施战略，以及它如何确保这些不成为被设限的资源。我们谈到的所有这些，都希望与世界共享。那我们就聊聊 JAX 和 StableHLO，以及开源整体的演进，还有这在今天为什么如此重要，能确保它不会变成被设限的资源。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think for us it's super important that we interact with the broader ecosystem and open source things so that people can, you know, see the source, they can modify it, they can help us improve it, and have it be a collaborative project that spans many, many organizations rather than just something we hold to ourselves — is super important. That's why we open source TensorFlow, why we open source JAX, why we open source sort of the StableHLO representation for the XLA compiler. And you know, we'll open source more things in the future. And we've been big contributors in general to open source — to the Linux kernel and so on for many years. And I think usually we're one of the larger organizations that contributes to collective open source efforts because we believe in that, and you know we think the whole ecosystem benefits when everyone works together.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得对我们来说，与更广泛的生态互动、把东西开源非常重要，这样人们能看到源码、能修改、能帮我们改进，让它成为一个跨越许多组织的协作项目，而不是只握在我们自己手里——这非常重要。这就是我们开源 TensorFlow、开源 JAX、开源 XLA 编译器所用的 StableHLO 表示的原因。未来我们还会开源更多东西。多年来我们一直是开源的大贡献者——对 Linux 内核等等。我觉得我们通常是参与集体开源项目最大的组织之一，因为我们相信这件事，我们认为当所有人一起合作时，整个生态都会受益。

turns.en: Yeah, it's a perfect segue for you to talk about PyTorch and your experience at Meta.
turns.zh: 这正好是个完美的过渡，让你谈谈 PyTorch 和你在 Meta 的经历。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, I was talking with Jeff right before this fireside chat. I think Jeff has been leading a lot of the AI infrastructure open source strategy. As Jeff mentioned, in the past Google open sourced TensorFlow and JAX, and Kubernetes also was created by Google and open sourced by Google, and Android, and a lot of awesome stuff. Then as now we push the TPU into the community and emphasize TPU on GCP, Google Cloud, we're even doubling down more on this open source strategy. So as a matter of fact, not only do we open source JAX, we also build up a lot of upper-level libraries — like how can we do the RL, we call Tunix, which is actually built upon JAX, we open source that too; how to do the checkpointing, how to do the inference stuff, we actually do a lot on top of JAX. We also build a lot of upper-level libraries and frameworks, and we're also open sourcing that because we want people using that and then leverage this open source strategy to use TPU directly. That's one thing. And of course we want to meet where the customer is, right? So we also want to embrace whatever mature products in the open source community. PyTorch is very mature, PyTorch is very widely used in the community. You know what, let's use PyTorch, let's embrace PyTorch on TPU. We actually have this project called torch TPU. We actually, right now in the private preview, we want to do the public preview next quarter, just in a couple months, and then in Q4 we want public offering — just on GitHub and everybody can use it. And yesterday, as I mentioned, if we use PyTorch TPU, it's just several simple lines of change — the backend device is TPU — then hopefully all the training and all the inference we just need to run on TPU. We actually support both eager mode and the compiled mode as well. That's on the frameworks level. And we also engage — I'm sure in the audience we have a lot of users using vLLM, we use SGLang — we also talk with the vLLM and SGLang teams to make sure this kind of open upper-level inference framework, open source framework, we can also use that on TPU as well. So a lot of work right now we're doing: we open source our own stuff, we also embrace the mature open source products in the community.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，就在这场炉边谈话之前我还在和 Jeff 聊。我觉得 Jeff 一直在主导很多 AI 基础设施的开源战略。正如 Jeff 所说，过去 Google 开源了 TensorFlow 和 JAX，Kubernetes 也是 Google 创造并开源的，还有 Android，以及很多很棒的东西。现在我们把 TPU 推向社区，在 Google Cloud（GCP）上强调 TPU，我们甚至更加加倍投入这一开源战略。所以事实上，我们不仅开源了 JAX，还构建了很多上层库——比如怎么做强化学习，我们叫 Tunix，它其实构建在 JAX 之上，我们也把它开源了；怎么做 checkpoint、怎么做推理相关的东西，我们在 JAX 之上做了很多。我们还构建了很多上层库和框架，也把它们开源，因为我们希望人们用起来，然后借这个开源战略直接使用 TPU。这是一方面。当然我们也想贴近客户所在之处，对吧？所以我们也想拥抱开源社区里成熟的产品。PyTorch 非常成熟，在社区里用得极广。你知道，那就用 PyTorch 吧，在 TPU 上拥抱 PyTorch。我们有个项目叫 torch TPU。目前是私有预览，我们想下季度做公开预览，就在几个月后，然后 Q4 做公开发布——就放在 GitHub 上，所有人都能用。昨天我也提到，如果用 PyTorch TPU，只需简单改几行——后端设备设成 TPU——那么希望所有训练和推理都只需在 TPU 上跑。我们其实同时支持 eager 模式和编译模式。这是在框架层面。我们也接触了——我相信观众里有很多用 vLLM 的用户，我们用 SGLang——我们也和 vLLM、SGLang 团队沟通，确保这类上层推理框架、开源框架也能在 TPU 上用。所以现在我们在做很多工作：我们开源自己的东西，也拥抱社区里成熟的开源产品。

turns.en: And then we do have a lot of first-year and second-year PhD students in the audience too. How many of you are PhD students? Okay. What are some of the things that they should be focusing on? Some of them are also undergrads too, just so you know.
turns.zh: 然后我们观众里还有很多一年级和二年级的博士生。你们有多少是博士生？好。他们应该关注些什么？顺便说一下，其中一些还是本科生。

turns.en: Okay. Yeah.
turns.zh: 好。是的。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean it's always exciting to be at that stage in your career because I think you can find things you really, really, really enjoy and think are important and figure out a way to push some area forward in terms of making an impact in the world. I think that's just a fun time.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，在职业生涯的那个阶段总是令人兴奋的，因为我认为你可以找到你真正、真正、真正喜欢并认为重要的事情，并找到一种方法推动某个领域向前发展，从而在世界上产生影响。我认为那只是一段有趣的时光。

turns.en: Is there like one physical bottleneck that you're thinking about just from an infrastructure perspective? There's so many.
turns.zh: 从基础设施的角度来看，你有没有考虑过某个物理瓶颈？有很多。

turns.en: Uh I mean I'm pretty bullish on more and more specialized hardware because I think that's the way you really get much more efficient systems. And we now have workloads where there's like a handful of workloads that are going to be a lot of the compute in the world, right? And so if you think about that, that is crying out for specialization. And the problem with specialization is if what you want to do changes in the future, then the thing you've lovingly crafted for in hardware for maybe two years is no longer perhaps as relevant. So I think to really make specialization work well, you need to automate much more of the hardware design process, right? Because right now the way you do hardware is you get a large team of people. Some of them take the high level spec and they build low-level RTL from it. Then because you've hand translated this, you end up with another team of people that are going to verify that the first team of people did the right thing. And then you're going to do another set of people who are going to lovingly lay out the chip. And you know that just seems like if you can make a lot more automated loops that are searchable by reinforcement learning or other evolutionary techniques perhaps, and you can make those loops run fast enough, which the current sort of EDA tools typically are not designed to run very quickly. But if you can make them run fast, then you have the opportunity to really have a much more automated exploration loop of the design process and perhaps to compress the design cycle tremendously. And if you could, for example, design a new chip with, you know, 10 people in three months instead of, you know, 150 people and two years,

So thinking in terms of like JAX or PyTorch expressions is what you want to do, not necessarily "how can I parallelize this with some kernel code" — be it a TPU kernel language or a GPU kernel language — in order to get maximum performance. That really, hopefully, the compiler and underlying system can give you that, and you can just think in beautiful abstractions like multiply.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，我也认为人们希望站在高得多的抽象层次上思考。所以用 JAX 或 PyTorch 表达式来思考才是你想做的，而不是去想“我怎么用某种 kernel 代码把它并行化”——不管是 TPU kernel 语言还是 GPU kernel 语言——来榨取最大性能。那真的应该、也希望能由编译器和底层系统来给你，而你只需要用像乘法这样漂亮的抽象来思考。

turns.en: Great to know. Thank you.
turns.zh: 很高兴了解这些。谢谢。

turns.en: I think we have time for one last question. Just one last question. Go ahead.
turns.zh: 我想我们还有时间回答最后一个问题。就最后一个问题。请讲。

turns.en: Okay. Hi, John from NYU. Been working on networking for many years. So I was very impressed by the talk, Bill, and the other fellow. So regarding the scalability here: I know these TPUs are connected in the 3D torus here, compared with other — you know, the UEC Ultra Ethernet consortium and so on — they are looking into this, you know, fabric across interconnection here. From the scalability point of view, do you see, when you scale up the GPU up to a few thousand or even one million here, whether this 3D torus is still able to handle all the communication at that large scale?
turns.zh: 好的。我是纽约大学的 John，做网络研究很多年了。Bill 和另一位讲者的演讲让我印象很深。关于这里的可扩展性：我知道这些 TPU 是通过 3D 环面（3D torus）连接的，而其他一些——比如 UEC 超以太网联盟等等——他们在研究跨互连的 fabric。从可扩展性的角度看，当你们把 GPU 扩展到几千甚至上百万颗芯片时，这个 3D 环面是否仍然能处理如此大规模下的所有通信？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I can say our largest pods for TPU v8, I believe, are 9,600-something chips. So that's the scale at which we do 3D tori. And then beyond that we have Pathways as a software abstraction on top of many of those 3D torus-connected pods, and that uses a data center network — whatever fabric you have in your data center — or even a multi-metro training setup where maybe you have five pods in this building in Oklahoma and eight more in this building in Iowa, and a high-speed WAN link between. So that seems to have worked pretty well for us for scaling up. And you do sometimes want to map the computation you're doing so that you have, for example, data parallel and model parallel dimensions, and you might typically want the model parallel aspect to be within a single pod or a slice of a pod, and then have data parallel replicas across those pods or slices of pods. And that seems to work pretty well for us. The nice thing about torus-based networks is they're super easy to connect locally, as opposed to needing very complicated wiring in your data center floor.
turns.zh: 是的，我可以这么说：我们 TPU v8 最大的 pod 我记得是 9,600 多颗芯片。这就是我们做 3D 环面的规模。再往上，我们有 Pathways 作为软件抽象，架在许多个 3D 环面连接的 pod 之上，它使用数据中心网络——你数据中心里有什么 fabric 就用什么——甚至可以是跨城训练部署，比如在俄克拉荷马这栋楼里有五个 pod，在爱荷华那栋楼里再有八个 pod，中间用高速广域网链路连起来。所以这对我们做规模扩张来说效果相当不错。而且你有时确实需要映射你的计算，比如有数据并行和模型并行两个维度，通常你会希望模型并行部分落在单个 pod 或 pod 的一个切片内，然后在那些 pod 或切片之间放数据并行副本。这对我们效果很好。基于环面的网络的好处是，本地连接超级容易，不需要在数据中心地面上做非常复杂的布线。

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Except for the funny mirrored optical switches.
turns.zh: 除了那些奇特的镜像光交换机。

turns.en: Anything to add, Bill?
turns.zh: Bill，有什么要补充的吗？

turns.en: Yeah, that's very much true. I think so. We have ICI within the rack, within the cube. Then we use the OCS to scale it up to 9,600. Then even going up, now we have — but actually got orchestrated by the Pathways software. Then going beyond 34,000 chips, we use data center networking to connect everything together. This kind of scalability — I think it's working pretty well for us.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。我认为是这样。我们在机架内、立方体内有 ICI。然后用 OCS 把它扩展到 9,600。再往上，现在我们有——但实际上是由 Pathways 软件来编排的。再超过 34,000 颗芯片，我们就用数据中心网络把所有东西连起来。这种可扩展性——我觉得对我们效果相当不错。

turns.en: Yeah. And I would say even at that scale, we're able to do fully synchronous training, which is nice from the ML reproducibility and interpretation standpoint. I think at some point asynchronous training will come back, but so far we've been able to push synchronous training quite far. And we'll see what happens.
turns.zh: 是的。而且我想说，即便在那个规模上，我们也能做完全同步的训练，这对机器学习的可复现性和可解释性来说很好。我认为某个时候异步训练会回归，但到目前为止我们已经把同步训练推得相当远了。我们拭目以待。

turns.en: That's a great way to end. We're out of time. Thank you so much, Jeff. Thank you, Bill, for your time. We have some really cool swag outside by the patio for you, which includes some famous Jeff Dean memes on a pen.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的收尾。我们时间到了。非常感谢你，Jeff。谢谢你，Bill，感谢你们抽时间。我们在外面露台边准备了一些很酷的周边给你们，其中包括印着著名 Jeff Dean 梗的笔。

turns.en: Tell me that.
turns.zh: 跟我说说那个。

turns.en: And a Dav Labs t-shirt.
turns.zh: 还有一件 Dav Labs 的 T 恤。

turns.en: Thank you. Great. Thanks so much, everybody.
turns.zh: 谢谢。太好了。非常感谢大家。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

consensus.en: Specialized hardware like TPUs is essential for efficient AI at scale, delivering major performance-per-watt gains.
consensus.zh: 像 TPU 这样的专用硬件对于高效的大规模 AI 至关重要，能带来显著的每瓦性能提升。

consensus.en: Co-designing models, hardware, compilers, and infrastructure under one roof accelerates progress.
consensus.zh: 在同一屋檐下协同设计模型、硬件、编译器和基础设施，能加速进展。

consensus.en: Reliability at 100k-chip scale is a system property, requiring robust software and operational practices.
consensus.zh: 在十万芯片规模下，可靠性是系统属性，需要稳健的软件和运维实践。

consensus.en: Open sourcing frameworks like JAX and embracing PyTorch prevents AI infrastructure from becoming gated.
consensus.zh: 开源 JAX 等框架并拥抱 PyTorch，可防止 AI 基础设施成为封闭资源。

consensus.en: Inference and training have different hardware needs; inference will increasingly dominate as agents mature.
consensus.zh: 推理和训练有不同的硬件需求；随着智能体成熟，推理将日益主导。

consensus.en: Automating hardware design with RL can compress chip design cycles and enable more specialization.
consensus.zh: 用强化学习自动化硬件设计可以缩短芯片设计周期，实现更多专用化。

contrarian.en: Commodity hardware scaling worked for search but not for AI training, which needs exotic interconnects.
contrarian.zh: 商品硬件扩展适用于搜索，但不适用于 AI 训练，后者需要特殊互连。

contrarian.en: Synchronous training can scale to tens of thousands of chips, contrary to assumptions favoring asynchronous.
contrarian.zh: 同步训练可以扩展到数万芯片，这与倾向于异步的假设相反。

contrarian.en: Agentic AI will expose that our tools are too slow, designed for human-speed iteration.
contrarian.zh: 智能体式 AI 将暴露我们的工具太慢，因为它们是为人类速度的迭代设计的。

contrarian.en: Code translation between languages is an effective agent task because the spec is fully specified.
contrarian.zh: 语言间的代码翻译是有效的智能体任务，因为规范是完全明确的。

contrarian.en: A rejected NeurIPS distillation paper became highly influential, showing peer review can miss impact.
contrarian.zh: 一篇被 NeurIPS 拒绝的蒸馏论文变得极具影响力，表明同行评审可能错过影响力。

contrarian.en: To make specialization work, we must automate hardware design loops to run much faster than EDA tools.
contrarian.zh: 要让专用化奏效，我们必须自动化硬件设计循环，使其运行得比 EDA 工具快得多。
